code.title: Declaration, expression and arrow functions

followUps:
A name on the function shows up in the stack trace, so you can see which function failed instead of "anonymous".

An unnamed function expression assigned to const f usually gets the name f automatically, but a callback passed inline (arr.map(function () {...})) has none. Naming it, e.g. function parseRow(...), labels the frame as parseRow. The name is also visible inside the function itself, which allows safe recursion even if the outer variable is reassigned.

It throws a TypeError ("add is not a constructor"), because arrows have no [[Construct]] behaviour and no prototype.

Example: const P = () => {}; new P(); fails immediately. Use a regular function or a class when you need to build objects with new. The same reason is why arrows cannot be generators and have no own this to bind to the new object.

Yes: wrap the object literal in parentheses, () => ({ ok: true }).

Without them the braces are read as a function body, so () => { ok: true } is a block containing the label ok and returns undefined. The parentheses force JavaScript to treat { ... } as an expression. Typical use: users.map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name })) turns 3 users into 3 small objects.

code.title: Pass by value: mutate vs reassign

followUps:
A swap function cannot work because the parameters are local copies of the values, so swapping them changes only the copies.

function swap(a, b) { const t = a; a = b; b = t; }
let x = 1, y = 2;
swap(x, y);   // x is still 1, y is still 2

To swap, either return the pair ([x, y] = [y, x] at the call site) or mutate a shared container, e.g. swap(arr, i, j) swapping two slots of an array. Cost is O(1) time and space.

Copy the data before the function touches it, or freeze it so mutation fails loudly.

Options: (1) work on a copy: const c = structuredClone(arg) for nested data, or [...arr] / { ...obj } for one level; (2) use non-mutating methods (toSorted, map, slice); (3) Object.freeze(arg) (shallow) so writes throw in strict mode. Example: sorting [3,1,2] with toSorted leaves the caller's array as [3,1,2].

Conceptually no: strings are immutable primitives, so it never matters whether the engine shares or copies them.

Engines like V8 often keep one copy of the characters and pass a pointer, because sharing is cheaper than copying a 1 MB string. But since you can never change the string in place (s[0] = "x" does nothing), the caller can never observe the sharing. Every "change" such as s + "!" creates a new string, so the behaviour is exactly that of pass-by-value.

code.title: slice copies, splice edits in place

followUps:
Use splice(2, 0, item): start at index 2, delete 0 items, insert the new one.

Example: const a = [10, 20, 30]; a.splice(2, 0, 25); makes a equal [10, 20, 25, 30] and returns [], since nothing was removed. It edits in place and shifts later items, so it is O(n). The non-mutating version is a.toSpliced(2, 0, 25) or [...a.slice(0, 2), 25, ...a.slice(2)].

It removes and returns the last element, so arr.splice(-1) behaves like pop() but returns an array.

A negative start counts from the end, and with no deleteCount everything from that point to the end is removed. With [1, 2, 3], splice(-1) returns [3] and leaves [1, 2]; splice(-2) would return [2, 3]. Compare slice(-1), which returns [3] but leaves the original untouched.

Build a new array without that item, using filter, slice or toSpliced, and leave the original alone.

const a = [10, 20, 30, 40];
a.filter((_, i) => i !== 1);        // [10, 30, 40]
a.toSpliced(1, 1);                  // [10, 30, 40]
[...a.slice(0, 1), ...a.slice(2)];  // [10, 30, 40]

All are O(n) time and O(n) space, and a still has 4 items afterwards. This is what React and Redux state updates need.

code.title: map vs forEach vs for...of with async

followUps:
In parallel use await Promise.all(items.map(asyncFn)); in sequence use for...of with await inside.

// parallel: all start at once
const out = await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne));
// sequence: one at a time
for (const id of ids) await fetchOne(id);

With 3 calls of 100 ms each, parallel takes about 100 ms and sequence about 300 ms. Parallel can overload a server for big lists, so limit concurrency in batches. forEach(async ...) is wrong for both because it does not wait.

Use some, every or find, which stop as soon as the answer is known, or use for...of with break.

Example on [1, 2, 3, 4]: find(x => x > 1) returns 2 after 2 checks; some(x => x === 3) stops at the third item; every(x => x < 3) stops at 3 and returns false. forEach, map and filter always visit every item; throwing an exception out of forEach is an ugly hack.

Both skip holes: the callback is never called for a missing index, but map keeps the hole in its result while forEach just does nothing.

For [1, , 3], forEach runs twice (indexes 0 and 2). map(x => x * 2) returns [2, <1 empty item>, 6], still length 3 with a hole at index 1. A hole is different from undefined, which is visited. Use Array.from or spread first if you want holes treated as undefined.

code.title: reduce: basics, map via reduce, spread trap

followUps:
Use reduce to build the output array by pushing the mapped value, starting from an empty array.

const map = (arr, f) =>
  arr.reduce((acc, x, i) => { acc.push(f(x, i, arr)); return acc; }, []);
map([1, 2, 3], x => x * 2); // [2, 4, 6]

It is O(n) time and O(n) space. Push into the same accumulator; [...acc, f(x)] would copy it every step and become O(n²).

reduceRight folds from the last element to the first, which is useful when order matters, such as building right-nested results.

Examples: reversing while concatenating, ["a","b","c"].reduceRight((s, x) => s + x, "") gives "cba"; composing functions so that compose(f, g, h)(x) is f(g(h(x))); or processing a stack-like list from the top. Same O(n) cost as reduce.

Because { ...acc, [k]: v } copies every existing key into a brand new object on each step, so the work grows with the size of the accumulator.

For n items the copies are 0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = about n²/2. With 10,000 items that is roughly 50 million property copies instead of 10,000 assignments, and it also produces lots of garbage. Fix: acc[k] = v; return acc; (O(n) total), or build a Map.

code.title: Default sort is by string; comparators

followUps:
Compare age first, and when the ages are equal fall through to the name using ||.

users.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));

a.age - b.age is 0 for ties, which is falsy, so the right side decides. For ages 30 (Cy), 25 (Al), 30 (Bo) the result is Al, Bo, Cy. Cost is O(n log n) comparisons. Because sort is stable, you could also sort by name first and then by age.

Because the comparator is inconsistent, so the shuffle is not uniform and some orders appear more often than others.

A valid comparator must give the same answer for the same pair, but a random one can say a < b and then b < a, and the sort algorithm (TimSort) was never designed for that. For a 3-item array, 6 orders should each appear 1/6 of the time; with this trick they do not. Use Fisher-Yates: for i from n-1 down to 1, swap a[i] with a[random 0..i]. It is O(n) and unbiased.

The sort stops working properly, because a boolean becomes 1 or 0 and never negative, so the engine never learns that a should come first.

(a, b) => a > b returns true (1) or false (0). Zero means "equal", so many pairs are treated as ties and the order stays wrong; the result depends on the engine. Always return a number: a - b or a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0.

code.title: Shallow vs deep copy

followUps:
Write a function that copies primitives directly and, for objects, records each original-to-copy pair in a WeakMap so a cycle is reused instead of looping forever.

function clone(x, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (x === null || typeof x !== "object") return x;
  if (seen.has(x)) return seen.get(x);
  const out = Array.isArray(x) ? [] : {};
  seen.set(x, out);
  for (const k of Object.keys(x)) out[k] = clone(x[k], seen);
  return out;
}

O(n) time and space; Dates, Maps and Sets need extra cases, or just use structuredClone.

Because updating immutably copies only the parts that changed, and unchanged parts keep the same reference, so React can detect changes with a cheap ===.

For { a: bigObj, count: 1 }, { ...state, count: 2 } makes one new top object and reuses bigObj, so only the top reference changed. A deep clone would copy everything every time (slow) and make every nested reference new, so every component would think its data changed and re-render.

No. Object.freeze is shallow, so nested objects stay changeable unless you freeze them too.

const o = Object.freeze({ a: { b: 1 } });
o.a.b = 2;   // works, o.a.b is now 2
o.a = null;  // ignored (throws in strict mode)

For a deep freeze, recurse over the values and freeze each object (O(n) over all nested values). Freezing does not clone anything either: other references to the same object see the frozen state.

code.title: Rest vs spread

followUps:
Because ...args is a real array with all array methods, while arguments is only an array-like object.

You can call args.map(...) or args.slice(1) directly; with arguments you must first convert it (Array.from(arguments)). Rest also shows in the signature that the function takes any number of values, works in arrow functions (which have no arguments), and combines with named parameters: f(first, ...others).

Yes: spreading a very large array into a call can throw a RangeError, because every element becomes a function argument and engines limit that count (often roughly 100,000 or more, depending on the stack size).

Math.max(...arr) with 500,000 numbers may fail. Use arr.reduce((m, x) => Math.max(m, x), -Infinity), which is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

{ ...null } gives an empty object {}, but [...null] throws a TypeError.

Object spread ignores null and undefined, which makes { ...defaults, ...maybeOptions } safe. Array spread needs an iterable and null is not one, so it fails with "not iterable". Guard with [...(list ?? [])].

code.title: Default parameter behaviour

followUps:
The old version replaced every falsy value, so a valid 0 was overwritten; a real default parameter only reacts to undefined.

function retries(n) { n = n || 10; return n; }  // retries(0) is 10, a bug
function retries(n = 10) { return n; }         // retries(0) is 0
// or: n ?? 10 to also cover null

The same bug hits '' and false. Use = default or ??.

Yes, a default can be any expression, including a function call, and it runs only when the argument is missing or undefined.

With function f(id = next()), calling f() twice runs next() twice, but f(100) never calls it. That makes defaults a neat place for required-argument checks, such as function f(x = required("x")) where required throws.

So that calling the function with no argument works: without it, destructuring undefined throws a TypeError.

function f({ retries = 3 }) {}      // f() throws
function g({ retries = 3 } = {}) {} // g() uses retries = 3

The = {} supplies an empty object when the whole argument is undefined, and then the inner defaults fill in each missing property. It does not help if the caller passes null.

code.title: What JSON.stringify loses

followUps:
Convert it to an array of entries for JSON.stringify, then rebuild it with new Map(...) in a reviver step or after parsing.

const m = new Map([["a", 1], ["b", 2]]);
const s = JSON.stringify([...m]);   // [["a",1],["b",2]]
const back = new Map(JSON.parse(s));

Plain JSON.stringify(m) gives {}, losing all data. A Set works the same with [...set] and new Set(arr). Both ways are O(n).

Try stringifying each top-level key on its own to see which one throws, then go deeper into that key; modern Node's error message also prints the path.

The message says things like "starting at object with constructor 'Object' --- property 'back' closes the circle". You can also pass a replacer that tracks a WeakSet of seen objects and returns "[Circular]" when it meets one again. For { ok: 1, loop: { back: root } } the culprit is loop.back.

Because valid JSON only proves the syntax is right, not that the data has the fields and types your code expects.

JSON.parse('{"age": "abc"}') succeeds, but age is a string, and later code like age + 1 gives "abc1". Data from users, files or the network can be missing fields, have wrong types or be hostile. Check the shape (by hand or with a schema library) right after parsing and reject bad input early.

code.title: Shallow and deep equality

followUps:
Because shallow comparison is very cheap, and React only needs to know whether something might have changed, not to inspect all the data.

Comparing references is O(1), while a deep comparison of a big object is O(size) on every render. React's rule is: never mutate, always create a new object when something changes. Then a different reference means a change, and the same reference means nothing changed. A mutation that keeps the same reference would be missed.

Object.is works like === except for two cases: NaN equals NaN, and +0 differs from -0.

NaN === NaN is false but Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true. 0 === -0 is true but Object.is(0, -0) is false. For every other value they give the same answer. Object.is is what React uses to compare state, and includes uses a similar rule (it finds NaN).

Return true if both are identical, otherwise check both are non-null objects with the same keys and Object.is-equal values.

function shallowEqual(a, b) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) return true;
  if (!a || !b || typeof a !== "object" || typeof b !== "object") return false;
  const ka = Object.keys(a), kb = Object.keys(b);
  return ka.length === kb.length && ka.every(k => Object.is(a[k], b[k]));
}

O(k) for k keys. shallowEqual({x:1},{x:1}) is true.

code.title: const, freeze, seal, preventExtensions

followUps:
Loop over the values, freeze each nested object first, then freeze the object itself.

function deepFreeze(o) {
  Object.values(o).forEach(v => {
    if (v && typeof v === "object") deepFreeze(v);
  });
  return Object.freeze(o);
}

It visits every nested value once, so O(n). Cycles are safe because already-frozen objects can be skipped with Object.isFrozen(v); add that check if your data might loop.

All three stop adding properties; they differ in how much more they lock.

  • preventExtensions: no new properties, but you can edit and delete existing ones.
  • seal: also no deleting, but values can be edited.
  • freeze: also no editing, the object is read-only.

Each is shallow. Check with Object.isExtensible, isSealed and isFrozen.

Not in any way you should rely on; freezing is for safety, not speed.

Engines can sometimes use the fact that a frozen object's shape will not change, but the gain is tiny and not guaranteed. Freezing itself costs time, which matters when you freeze thousands of objects recursively. Use it to catch accidental mutation bugs (in strict mode, a write throws a TypeError), and measure before claiming any speed benefit.

code.title: Sparse arrays and holes

followUps:
The map callback skips holes, and new Array(3) has three holes and no real elements, so the callback never runs and the result is still three empty slots.

new Array(3) only sets length to 3. Fix it by making real elements first: Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i) gives [0, 1, 2], or new Array(3).fill(0).map((_, i) => i), or [...Array(3).keys()].

indexOf never finds NaN and skips holes, while includes finds NaN and treats holes as undefined.

[NaN].indexOf(NaN)       // -1  (uses ===)
[NaN].includes(NaN)      // true
[, 1].indexOf(undefined) // -1  (hole skipped)
[, 1].includes(undefined)// true

Prefer includes for membership checks, and findIndex(Number.isNaN) when you need the position of NaN.

Elements kinds are the internal storage types V8 picks for arrays, which decide how fast array code runs.

The main ones are SMI (small integers), DOUBLE (floating point) and generic ELEMENTS (any value), each with a HOLEY variant for arrays with holes. An array only moves toward the more general kind, never back: [1, 2] (SMI) becomes DOUBLE after pushing 1.5, and generic after pushing a string. Keeping arrays of one type and without holes lets V8 use its fastest paths.

code.title: References and spooky bugs

followUps:
The array is one object on the heap, and the variable grid holds three slots that all point to that single inner array.

Array(3).fill([]) evaluates [] once and copies the reference into each slot. So grid[0].push(1) changes the shared array, and grid prints [[1],[1],[1]]. Memory: grid -> [ref, ref, ref], each ref -> the same inner array. Fix: Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => []) creates three separate arrays.

An object can be garbage collected once nothing reachable can get to it any more.

The engine starts from roots (global variables, the current call stack) and follows references; whatever is not reached is unreachable and its memory is freed. After let o = { big: 1 }; o = null; the object has no references left and is eligible. Two objects that point only at each other are still collected if no root reaches them, because modern collectors use reachability, not reference counts.

A WeakMap holds its keys weakly: it does not count as a reference, so it never keeps the key object alive.

If you do wm.set(obj, meta) and later nothing else references obj, the object and its entry can both be collected. That makes WeakMap good for attaching private data or caches to objects without causing memory leaks. Keys must be objects, and you cannot iterate or get the size, since entries may vanish at any time.

code.title: Pipeline cost, early exit, Set lookup

followUps:
Use the browser or Node profiler to measure where time really goes, then optimise only that part.

In Chrome DevTools: Performance tab, record while running the code, and look at the flame chart for the functions with the most self time. In Node: node --prof app.js then node --prof-process, or node --cpu-prof and open the file in DevTools. For quick checks, console.time("x") around a run of 100,000 items works. Repeat the run several times, because the first run includes warm-up.

Iterator helpers are methods like map, filter and take that work on iterators and process one item at a time, only when you ask for the next value.

With arr.values().filter(f).map(g).take(2).toArray() on a million items, the pipeline pulls items one by one and stops after 2 results, never creating a full intermediate array. Plain array methods are eager: each step finishes the whole array before the next starts. Needs Node 22 or a recent browser.

A Set lookup is faster when you check many items, because has takes about O(1) while includes scans the array in O(n).

Checking 3,000 items against another list of 3,000 with includes is up to 9 million comparisons; building a Set costs 3,000 steps and then 3,000 O(1) lookups. The Set uses a hash table, so it jumps straight to the right bucket. For a handful of items, includes is as fast and uses no extra memory.

code.title: Group, count and index with Map and groupBy

followUps:
Because a plain object would inherit keys like toString and constructor from Object.prototype, which would clash with group names.

With a normal {}, groups.constructor already exists even when no item has that key, so if (groups[key]) checks lie. A null-prototype object has no inherited properties, so only real groups appear and "constructor" is just another name. The trade-off: it lacks methods such as hasOwnProperty, so use Object.hasOwn(g, k) or k in g.

Use a Map when keys are not strings, when you add and remove keys often, or when you need to count items and keep insertion order.

A Map accepts any key type (objects, numbers kept as numbers), has .size, iterates in insertion order and has no inherited keys. In a plain object, obj[1] and obj["1"] are the same key, and a key like "__proto__" can cause trouble. Use a plain object for fixed, known fields (a record) and JSON data.

JSON cannot hold a Map directly, so turn it into an array of [key, value] pairs, stringify that, and rebuild with new Map.

const m = new Map([[1, "a"], [2, "b"]]);
const json = JSON.stringify([...m]);      // [[1,"a"],[2,"b"]]
const back = new Map(JSON.parse(json));   // Map(2)

Number keys stay numbers this way. With Object.fromEntries(m) the keys become strings ("1"), and non-string keys are lost.
